metadata.vertical_interpretation: Illustrative height above the mapped ellipsoid. Published MSL or AGL altitudes are used as approximate local height because this prototype has no detailed terrain model.
metadata.warning: These are not observed altitude traces. Only a few event heights are documented; all other point heights are interpolated estimates from aircraft performance and flight context.
metadata.units: lon degrees, lat degrees, estimated height metres

properties.title: Wright Flyer — first powered flight
properties.route_summary: First Flight Boulder → first landing marker, Kill Devil Hills
properties.overview: On 17 December 1903, Orville Wright piloted the Wright Flyer from level ground at Kill Devil Hills while Wilbur ran alongside. The aircraft remained airborne for 12 seconds and traveled 120 feet; the brothers completed three additional flights later that day.
properties.why_famous: It is widely recognized as the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft.
properties.description: The 120-foot, 12-second first flight. The line connects the preserved launch and landing markers; it is not a telemetry trace.
properties.source_title: National Park Service — First Flight Landing

altitude_estimate.basis: NPS reports the first hop about 8 feet above the ground; a low smooth arc connects takeoff and landing.

properties.title: Spirit of St. Louis — solo Atlantic crossing
properties.route_summary: Roosevelt Field, New York → Ireland → southwest Britain → Le Bourget, Paris
properties.overview: Charles Lindbergh flew the single-engine Spirit of St. Louis alone from Long Island to Paris in 33½ hours. He crossed the Atlantic without radio navigation, relying on dead reckoning and visual landmarks.
properties.why_famous: The first solo nonstop transatlantic flight made Lindbergh an international celebrity and helped accelerate public acceptance of long-distance aviation.
properties.description: Intermediate landfall areas follow the Smithsonian account. The connecting curves are illustrative reconstructions, not a recorded flight track.
properties.source_title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum — Spirit of St. Louis

altitude_estimate.basis: The Smithsonian describes a surviving barograph with climbs for weather, turbulence-induced drops, and descent near Ireland, but not digitized point heights. Control heights are illustrative.

properties.title: Enola Gay — Hiroshima mission
properties.route_summary: Tinian → Iwo Jima rendezvous → Hiroshima → return via Iwo Jima → Tinian
properties.overview: Enola Gay was a U.S. Army Air Forces B-29 commanded by Paul Tibbets. On 6 August 1945 it flew from Tinian to Hiroshima and released the uranium bomb Little Boy, destroying much of the city and killing tens of thousands of people before returning to Tinian.
properties.why_famous: It carried out the first atomic bombing in warfare, an event that transformed military history and began the nuclear age.
properties.description: The navigator's surviving log supplies the rendezvous, target, return positions, and times. Lines between logged positions are reconstructed.
properties.source_title: National Museum of Nuclear Science & History — Hiroshima Log

altitude_estimate.basis: The Smithsonian documents a 31,000-foot bomb release over Hiroshima. Other heights are smooth B-29 climb, cruise, and return estimates.

properties.title: Amelia Earhart — solo Atlantic crossing
properties.route_summary: Harbour Grace, Newfoundland → Culmore near Derry, Northern Ireland
properties.overview: Amelia Earhart departed Newfoundland in a Lockheed Vega intending to reach Paris. Ice, poor weather, an exhaust fire, and instrument problems forced her to land in a field near Derry after almost fifteen hours in the air.
properties.why_famous: Earhart became the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic and only the second person to do so after Lindbergh.
properties.description: Earhart intended to reach Paris but landed near Derry. No continuous position record is asserted here.
properties.source_title: NASA — Realizing the Dream of Flight

altitude_estimate.basis: Lockheed Vega-era cruise-height reconstruction; no continuous altimeter record has been incorporated.

properties.title: Bell X-1 — first supersonic flight
properties.quality_label: Documented local profile; illustrative plan-view path
properties.route_summary: Muroc Army Air Field → B-29 air launch over Muroc Dry Lake → Rogers Dry Lake landing
properties.overview: A Boeing B-29 carried the rocket-powered Bell X-1 to launch altitude over California's Mojave Desert. Chuck Yeager then accelerated the aircraft to Mach 1.06 before gliding back to the dry lakebed.
properties.why_famous: It was the first piloted aircraft flight conclusively measured above the speed of sound in level flight.
properties.description: NASA documents the carrier takeoff, air launch, speed run, and glide landing area. The exact plan-view curve is illustrative.
properties.source_title: NASA — Research in Supersonic Flight

anchors.name: X-1 air-launch area
anchors.note: Approximate drop area over the dry lake

altitude_estimate.basis: NASA reports the B-29 carrier at about 20,000 feet; NASA's X-1 account gives an approximately 43,000-foot test height. The carrier segment and rocket climb are generalized.

properties.title: US Airways 1549 — Hudson River ditching
properties.route_summary: LaGuardia Runway 4 → bird encounter north of the Bronx → Hudson River ditching
properties.overview: Shortly after takeoff, the Airbus A320 struck a flock of Canada geese and lost effective thrust from both engines. Captain Chesley Sullenberger and First Officer Jeffrey Skiles ditched the aircraft in the Hudson River, where nearby vessels assisted the evacuation.
properties.why_famous: All 155 occupants survived a dual-engine failure and water landing in the center of New York City, leading the event to be called the “Miracle on the Hudson.”
properties.description: Runway points lead into 19 sampled NTSB secondary-radar returns (15:25:59–15:30:27 EST). The last two positions are NTSB estimates of touchdown and where the aircraft stopped. Curves between these positions are interpolated, not raw flight-data-recorder telemetry; radar range accuracy is about ±380 ft.
properties.source_title: NTSB — US1549 Aircraft Performance Factual Report, Table 1a

Intermediate heights are interpolated; the runway and ditching anchors are grounded estimates. Mode C is coarse MSL pressure altitude, not exact height above terrain or an FDR trace.

properties.title: Concorde BA300 — inaugural commercial service
properties.route_summary: London Heathrow → Bahrain International Airport
properties.overview: British Airways flight BA300 carried fare-paying passengers from London to Bahrain on Concorde's first day of scheduled operation. An Air France Concorde simultaneously began service from Paris toward Rio de Janeiro via Dakar.
properties.why_famous: The paired inaugural services opened the era of scheduled supersonic passenger travel.
properties.description: The commercial endpoints are documented by British Airways. The line is a geodesic reconstruction, not an operational flight plan.
properties.source_title: British Airways — Celebrating Concorde

altitude_estimate.basis: British Airways gives Concorde a cruise capability up to 60,000 feet; this first London-Bahrain service is illustrated with a 55,000-foot cruise estimate.

properties.title: Rutan Voyager — nonstop unrefueled circumnavigation
properties.route_summary: Edwards AFB → westbound Pacific, Asia, Indian Ocean, Africa, Atlantic and Caribbean → Edwards AFB
properties.overview: Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager flew the lightweight composite Voyager westward around the globe, remaining airborne for just over nine days. They endured storms, equipment problems, extreme fatigue, and dwindling fuel reserves before returning to Edwards Air Force Base.
properties.why_famous: Voyager completed the first nonstop, unrefueled circumnavigation of Earth by an aircraft.
properties.description: The broad corridor follows a 1987 map credited to the Voyager project's meteorologists, with named places represented by approximate map positions. It is not a sequence of recorded GPS fixes or a navigation-quality track.
properties.source_title: DiBiase and Krygier — 1987 Voyager flight-data map

anchors.name: Indian Ocean south of Sri Lanka
Lake Victoria / Entebbe vicinity
anchors.note: Named overflight on 1987 flight-data map; Entebbe is a geographic proxy

altitude_estimate.basis: Smithsonian reports an 8,000-foot economical height, 20,500 feet over Africa to avoid storms, and 3,500 feet after a late engine emergency. The intervening heights are inferred.

properties.title: Alcock and Brown — first nonstop Atlantic crossing
properties.route_summary: St. John's, Newfoundland → Derrigimlagh Bog near Clifden, Ireland
properties.overview: John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown crossed the North Atlantic in a modified Vickers Vimy bomber. After more than sixteen hours in fog, icing, and equipment failures, they crash-landed in an Irish bog without serious injury.
properties.why_famous: Their journey was the first nonstop transatlantic flight, eight years before Lindbergh's better-known solo crossing.
properties.description: The endpoints are authoritative; the ocean segment is a great-circle reconstruction rather than a recorded track.
properties.source_title: Royal Air Force — First Non-stop Flight
properties.wiki_title: Transatlantic flight of Alcock and Brown

altitude_estimate.basis: Illustrative low-thousands-of-feet cruise for the modified Vickers Vimy; the RAF source confirms the flight, not a continuous height trace.

properties.title: Blériot XI — first airplane crossing of the Channel
properties.route_summary: Les Baraques near Calais → St. Margaret's Bay → Northfall Meadow, Dover
properties.overview: Louis Blériot flew his small Blériot XI monoplane from the French coast to England in roughly 37 minutes. Without a compass, he followed ships across the Channel and the English coastline to a landing near Dover Castle.
properties.why_famous: It was the first airplane crossing of the English Channel and demonstrated aviation's ability to connect countries across open water.
properties.description: Dover Museum records Blériot's wind-driven landfall at St. Margaret's Bay before he followed the coast to Dover.
properties.source_title: Dover Museum — Louis Blériot Landing in Dover

altitude_estimate.basis: A low-level Channel crossing is inferred from the early monoplane and the documented short route; no point altitudes are claimed.

properties.title: Vin Fiz — first U.S. transcontinental flight
properties.route_summary: Sheepshead Bay → Midwest → Kansas City → Texas → southern border corridor → Pasadena → Long Beach
properties.overview: Calbraith Perry Rodgers crossed the United States in the Wright EX Vin Fiz with support from a special train carrying mechanics and spare parts. The trip took 49 days and involved numerous crashes, forced landings, and repairs.
properties.why_famous: It was the first transcontinental flight across the United States, showing both the promise and fragility of early long-distance aviation.
properties.description: Smithsonian documents the broad route and finish. Selected major stops define this generalized reconstruction; the actual journey involved many more forced landings.
properties.source_title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum — Wright EX Vin Fiz

altitude_estimate.basis: Smithsonian records a 4,000-foot height near Imperial Junction; elsewhere short low-level legs are inferred. Named stops are treated as landings for illustration.

properties.title: St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line — inaugural flight
properties.route_summary: St. Petersburg waterfront → Tampa waterfront across Tampa Bay
properties.overview: Tony Jannus piloted a Benoist XIV flying boat across Tampa Bay with former St. Petersburg mayor Abram Pheil as its first paying passenger. The regularly scheduled service reduced a lengthy surface journey to about 23 minutes.
properties.why_famous: The flight inaugurated the world's first scheduled passenger airline using a fixed-wing aircraft.
properties.description: The 18-mile scheduled route is documented by the Smithsonian. The exact water track is reconstructed.
properties.source_title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum — Early Airlines

altitude_estimate.basis: Illustrative low-height Benoist flying-boat crossing of Tampa Bay; the source gives duration and route but no altimeter trace.

properties.title: Douglas World Cruisers — first aerial circumnavigation
properties.route_summary: Seattle → Aleutians → Japan → South Asia → Europe → North Atlantic → North America → Seattle
properties.overview: Four U.S. Army Air Service Douglas World Cruisers left Seattle on a westbound global expedition supported by ships, fuel caches, and maintenance depots. Two original aircraft, Chicago and New Orleans, completed the 175-day journey.
properties.why_famous: It was the first successful aerial circumnavigation of the world and a landmark demonstration of global flight logistics.
properties.description: Major landing and support points follow National Archives and U.S. Navy expedition accounts. The Nikolski Bay weather diversion and two intervening Japanese landfalls are included; many minor stops and local repositioning flights are omitted. Coordinates are named-place proxies, not flight fixes.
properties.source_title: National Archives — Magellans of the Sky

anchors.name: Nikolski Bay, Commander Islands
anchors.note: Unplanned May 15–16 weather-diversion landing; harbor location approximate

anchors.name: Ōminato, Honshū
anchors.note: May 22 landing; modern port-area geographic proxy, not a 1924 mooring position

altitude_estimate.basis: Illustrative 1924 biplane cruise heights between named stations. Some anchors were overflights rather than stops, so local descents should not be read as a flight log.

properties.title: Southern Cross — first U.S.–Australia trans-Pacific flight
properties.route_summary: Oakland → Wheeler Field → Barking Sands → Suva → Naselai Beach → Brisbane
properties.overview: Charles Kingsford Smith, Charles Ulm, Harry Lyon, and James Warner flew the Fokker trimotor Southern Cross from California to Australia in three principal oceanic stages. The Hawaii-to-Fiji leg was then the longest flight made over water.
properties.why_famous: The expedition completed the first trans-Pacific flight from the continental United States to Australia.
properties.description: All principal stops and the Fiji repositioning are represented; connecting curves are illustrative reconstructions, not observed tracks.
properties.source_title: National Museum of Australia — Charles Ulm Collection

altitude_estimate.basis: Illustrative Fokker trimotor cruise and landing transitions on documented legs; no recorded heights were recovered.

properties.title: Wiley Post — first solo circumnavigation
properties.route_summary: Floyd Bennett Field → Berlin → Königsberg → Moscow → Novosibirsk → Irkutsk → Rukhlovo → Khabarovsk → Flat → Fairbanks → Edmonton → Floyd Bennett Field
properties.overview: Wiley Post flew the Lockheed Vega Winnie Mae alone around the Northern Hemisphere, aided by an early autopilot and radio direction finder. Repairs and an emergency landing in Alaska interrupted the journey, which still took less than eight days.
properties.why_famous: Post became the first person to fly solo around the world and demonstrated the value of emerging navigation and automatic-control technology.
properties.description: Stops follow the Smithsonian's comparison of Post's 1931 and 1933 itineraries and its 1933 account. It reports two unlocated poor-visibility landings between Moscow and Novosibirsk; no positions are inferred for them. Coordinates mark named places, and connecting curves are illustrative reconstructions. The Winnie Mae landed at Flat, was repaired there, then followed Joe Crosson to Fairbanks for fuel; the replacement propeller was flown separately from Fairbanks to Flat.
properties.source_title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum — Mohler & Johnson, Wiley Post (1971)

anchors.name: Berlin Tempelhof
anchors.note: Reached nonstop from Floyd Bennett on July 16, 1933.

anchors.name: Königsberg
anchors.note: Unscheduled landing after Post turned back for missing maps; grounded overnight by weather.

anchors.name: Moscow
anchors.note: Unscheduled landing for Sperry autopilot repair.

anchors.name: Novosibirsk
anchors.note: The Smithsonian account reports two additional poor-visibility landings between Moscow and here, but gives no locations.

anchors.name: Irkutsk
anchors.note: Unscheduled landing for further autopilot repairs.

anchors.name: Rukhlovo (now Skovorodino)
anchors.note: Named stop; coordinates printed in the Smithsonian itinerary.

anchors.name: Flat, Alaska
anchors.note: Emergency landing and repairs after a nose-over; replacement propeller was flown here from Fairbanks.

anchors.name: Fairbanks, Alaska
anchors.note: The repaired Winnie Mae followed Joe Crosson here and refueled; the replacement propeller had been flown separately from Fairbanks to Flat.

altitude_estimate.basis: The 1933 flight predated Post's 1935 pressure-suit stratospheric experiments. Heights are conservative Vega cruise estimates between stops, not the later 30,000-foot research profile.

properties.title: China Clipper — inaugural trans-Pacific airmail flight
properties.route_summary: Alameda → Hawaiʻi → Midway → Wake → Guam → Manila
properties.overview: Pan American Airways' Martin M-130 China Clipper carried mail from San Francisco Bay to Manila by island-hopping through newly developed Pacific bases. The journey took approximately one week and crossed the ocean in five long stages.
properties.why_famous: It inaugurated regular trans-Pacific airmail service and established the route later used by Pan Am's celebrated passenger Clippers.
properties.description: The National Park Service documents the island refueling chain and Alameda-to-Manila inaugural service.
properties.source_title: National Park Service — Pan American Airways in the Pacific

altitude_estimate.basis: Illustrative Martin M-130 cruise between documented Pacific refueling stops; no altitude log is asserted.

properties.title: Hughes H-4 Hercules — the Spruce Goose's only flight
properties.route_summary: Short takeoff and landing run within Long Beach Harbor
properties.overview: During a taxi test in Long Beach Harbor, Howard Hughes lifted the enormous wooden H-4 Hercules flying boat from the water for about 30 seconds. The prototype landed safely and was maintained for decades but never flew again.
properties.why_famous: The brief hop was the only flight of the “Spruce Goose,” one of the largest aircraft ever built and an enduring symbol of Howard Hughes' ambition.
properties.description: The museum documents a roughly 30-second flight just under half a mile. Exact liftoff and touchdown coordinates are approximate.
properties.source_title: Evergreen Aviation & Space Museum — The Spruce Goose

altitude_estimate.basis: The aircraft's museum reports about 25 feet over the harbor during its brief hop.

properties.title: Pan Am — first commercial Boeing 747 flight
properties.route_summary: New York–JFK → London Heathrow
properties.overview: Pan American World Airways introduced the Boeing 747 into revenue service on an overnight flight from New York to London. The inaugural departure was delayed by mechanical trouble and ultimately operated by a substitute 747.
properties.why_famous: The flight opened the jumbo-jet era, greatly increasing long-haul passenger capacity and helping make intercontinental travel more accessible.
properties.description: Boeing documents the city-pair. The displayed line is a great-circle reconstruction rather than the historical clearance route.
properties.source_title: Boeing — 747 history

altitude_estimate.basis: A 35,000-foot long-haul 747-100 cruise is estimated from type performance; the inaugural flight's actual cleared levels are not known.

properties.title: Gossamer Albatross — human-powered Channel crossing
properties.route_summary: Folkestone, England → Cap Gris-Nez, France
properties.overview: Cyclist and pilot Bryan Allen powered Paul MacCready's ultralight Gossamer Albatross across the English Channel by pedaling for nearly three hours. The aircraft landed on a beach at Cap Gris-Nez after covering 36.2 kilometers.
properties.why_famous: It was the first successful English Channel crossing by a human-powered aircraft and won the second Kremer Prize.
properties.description: The Smithsonian documents both endpoints and the 36.2 km distance. The intermediate line is reconstructed.
properties.source_title: Smithsonian — MacCready Gossamer Albatross

altitude_estimate.basis: The human-powered Channel flight is shown only a few metres over water; Smithsonian confirms the route but does not provide an altitude trace.

properties.title: Solar Impulse 2 — first solar-powered circumnavigation
properties.route_summary: Abu Dhabi → Asia → Hawaiʻi → continental U.S. → Europe → Cairo → Abu Dhabi
properties.overview: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg alternated as pilots of Solar Impulse 2 during a 17-leg journey around the Northern Hemisphere. The aircraft used solar cells to power electric motors and recharge its batteries for overnight flight.
properties.why_famous: It completed the first circumnavigation by a piloted solar-powered fixed-wing aircraft without consuming aviation fuel.
properties.description: All 17 legs come from the mission's official route record. Connecting curves between airports are illustrative interpolations, not recorded flight tracks. Abu Dhabi endpoints use the official Al Bateen airport reference point.
properties.source_title: Solar Impulse — Around the World Adventure; UAE GCAA AIP OMAD

anchors.name: Al Bateen Executive Airport, Abu Dhabi
anchors.note: GCAA AIP OMAD airport reference point.

anchors.name: Al Bateen Executive Airport, Abu Dhabi
anchors.note: GCAA AIP OMAD airport reference point.

altitude_estimate.basis: The mission gives 8,500 metres maximum cruising altitude and a day-climb/night-descent strategy. Cycles are schematic because point timestamps are unavailable.

properties.title: NC-4 — first aircraft across the Atlantic
properties.route_summary: Rockaway → New England and Newfoundland → Azores → Lisbon → Ferrol → Plymouth
properties.overview: Between 8 and 31 May 1919, the U.S. Navy flying boat NC-4 made the first successful Atlantic crossing by aircraft. Commanded by Albert C. Read, it departed New York with NC-1 and NC-3, but mechanical trouble delayed it and the other aircraft were lost after forced landings. Guided across the ocean by a chain of Navy ships, NC-4 reached the Azores, landed at Lisbon on 27 May, and continued to Plymouth.
properties.why_famous: It was the first aircraft to cross the Atlantic and the first to fly from the United States to England, two weeks before the first nonstop crossing.
properties.description: The Navy documents the stop sequence and dates. Coordinates represent historic stations, harbors, or river mouths rather than exact takeoff and alighting positions.
properties.source_title: U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command — H-Gram 030: NC-4

altitude_estimate.basis: The Navy lists a 4,500-foot ceiling; lower typical flying-boat cruise is inferred between documented harbor landings.

properties.title: Graf Zeppelin — first airship circumnavigation
properties.route_summary: Lakehurst → Friedrichshafen → Siberia → Tokyo → Los Angeles → U.S. cities → Lakehurst
properties.overview: Under Hugo Eckener, the rigid airship LZ 127 Graf Zeppelin circled the Northern Hemisphere with passengers, crew, journalists, mail, and scientific observers aboard. The Lakehurst circuit stopped only at Friedrichshafen, Kasumigaura near Tokyo, and Mines Field in Los Angeles. Weather repeatedly altered the intended track over Siberia and the North Pacific. The voyage finished in about three weeks, with roughly twelve days airborne.
properties.why_famous: It was the first passenger-carrying flight around the world, set a new circumnavigation speed record, and made the first nonstop Pacific crossing by an aircraft.
properties.description: Landing stations and many named overflights are documented. Siberian, mountain, ocean-approach, and city-center anchors shape a weather-altered corridor rather than reproduce a position log.
properties.source_title: Smithsonian — Graf Zeppelin 1929 World Flight

anchors.name: Verkhneimbatsk, Siberia
anchors.note: Approximate match for Imbatsk radio station

altitude_estimate.basis: The Stanovoy crossing is reported near 6,000 feet; ordinary airship heights are illustrative. Only documented landing stations are treated as stops.

properties.title: Lucky Lady II — first nonstop flight around the world
properties.route_summary: Carswell AFB → Azores → Arabia → Philippines → Hawaiʻi → Carswell AFB without landing
properties.overview: Lucky Lady II was a U.S. Air Force B-50A commanded by James Gallagher. Departing Carswell Air Force Base on 26 February 1949, its fourteen-person crew flew eastward around the globe and returned after 94 hours and 1 minute aloft. Four aerial-refueling rendezvous—over the Azores, Saudi Arabia, the Philippines, and Hawaiʻi—made the 23,452-mile flight possible without landing.
properties.why_famous: It completed the first nonstop aircraft circumnavigation and demonstrated that aerial refueling could give strategic aircraft global reach.
properties.description: Official histories identify broad refueling regions, not exact tanker rendezvous coordinates. Intermediate airfields are geographic proxies and were not landing stops.
properties.source_title: U.S. Air Force Historical Support Division — Lucky Ladies I, II and III

altitude_estimate.basis: B-50 cruise and four aerial-refueling regions are documented, but refueling altitudes are not. A roughly 20,000-foot cruise with shallow refueling descents is illustrative.

properties.title: SR-71 Blackbird — coast-to-coast retirement record
properties.route_summary: Palmdale → offshore running start → Los Angeles → Kansas City → St. Louis → Cincinnati → Dulles
properties.overview: On 6 March 1990, U.S. Air Force SR-71A 61-7972 left Plant 42 at Palmdale for delivery to the Smithsonian. Raymond Yeilding and Joseph Vida refueled over the Pacific, made a 200-mile running start, crossed the coast above Mach 2.5, and reached Mach 3.3 and 83,000 feet. The flight established four recognized-course records before landing at Washington Dulles and entering the national collection.
properties.why_famous: Its 67-minute 54-second coast-to-coast flight and 64-minute 20-second Los Angeles-to-Washington run remain spectacular demonstrations of Blackbird performance.
properties.description: Origin, destination, performance, and named record segments are documented. City coordinates represent course benchmarks, not a published radar track; the offshore refueling loop is omitted.
properties.source_title: Beale Air Force Base — SR-71 sets records

anchors.name: Oxnard coast benchmark
anchors.note: Representative coast point after offshore running start

altitude_estimate.basis: The Air Force documents SR-71 high-altitude capability; 80,000 feet is a representative record-run height, not a published altimeter trace for 6 March 1990.

properties.title: Air Canada 143 — the Gimli Glider
properties.route_summary: Montréal → Ottawa → Red Lake area → Winnipeg diversion → powerless landing at Gimli
properties.overview: Air Canada Flight 143 was a Boeing 767 scheduled from Montréal to Edmonton via Ottawa. An incorrect fuel-unit conversion left it with roughly half the fuel believed to be aboard. Both engines stopped after warnings near Red Lake during a diversion toward Winnipeg. Captain Robert Pearson and First Officer Maurice Quintal redirected to the former RCAF station at Gimli and glided the powerless jet onto a decommissioned runway used as a motorsport track.
properties.why_famous: All 69 occupants survived the fuel-starved wide-body’s powerless landing, earning the aircraft its enduring nickname, the “Gimli Glider.”
properties.description: The official inquiry documents the airport sequence, Red Lake region, diversion, distances, and landing. Intermediate event points are approximate geometric proxies, not recorder coordinates.
properties.source_title: Government of Canada Board of Inquiry — Air Canada Flight 143

anchors.name: Red Lake area
anchors.note: Locale proxy for reported fuel-exhaustion region

anchors.name: Dual-engine flameout area
anchors.note: Approximate distance-intersection proxy: inquiry says 65 mi from Winnipeg and 45 mi from Gimli at 35,000 ft

anchors.name: Gimli redirect area
anchors.note: Approximate proxy for inquiry's 12 mi to Gimli at 20:32 CDT; not a recorded position

altitude_estimate.basis: FAA reports a 41,000-foot cruise, first engine loss during descent, and second engine loss at 35,000 feet. The final powerless glide is estimated to the Gimli landing.
